name: Northwestern Game Jam
oneLiner: A horror game built in Unity: A college amateur exorcist hired to cleanse a haunted show home, only to uncover the unsettling story of its former resident.

context.partner: Northwestern Game Jam 2026 · theme “Twist of Fate”
context.role: Concept & narrative designer, Unity developer — pitch, design documents, in-game writing, gameplay scripting, 3D assets

brief.problem: Five weeks, the theme Twist of Fate, a showcase on May 9 — my first video game. A college student with a side hustle in Daoist rituals is paid $5,000 to cleanse a staged house that keeps scaring buyers away. The ghost is the last resident, who refused to sell.
brief.solution: Candell Handles, a first-person horror game in Unity: a ghost cat leads you through the house, letters tell the story, a grandmother hunts you on sight. About 6,000 lines of our own C# on a horror template; props from Tripo, characters from Mixamo. I did concept, narrative, in-game writing, gameplay scripting and 3D assets.
brief.impact: Two endings: a pistol with one bullet, or five charms dropped in the pool to set her free. Two days before the showcase Unity would only open in Safe Mode with 999+ errors; we fixed it on May 8 and demoed to four judges on May 9.

blocks.title: A ghost story about who owns a house
blocks.text:
Northwestern Game Jam 2026 gave teams five weeks, the theme Twist of Fate and a showcase on May 9. The four of us ended up with **Candell Handles**. A college student with a side hustle in Daoist rituals gets a call from a developer: a staged, move-in-ready house keeps scaring buyers away, and they will pay $5,000 to make it stop by Friday night.

The ghost is the last resident, who refused to sell and died there. The twist belongs to the exorcist: she thinks she was hired to solve a problem, and she is the last step of it.

media.caption: Title screen: Candell’s dorm desk, the talismans buried under pizza and soda cans.

blocks.title: Rules borrowed from Parasite and Papers, Please
blocks.text: Our references were films and games. **Parasite** gave every version its question: the people living inside a house may have more claim to it than the person on the paperwork. **Papers, Please** gave the Airbnb version its verb: read a booking request, approve or deny it, live with the money. In the realtor version, house hunters were to chatter like the radio in Two Point Hospital, chipper and deadpan.

media.caption: <Papers, Please>, the game we referenced, centers on reading and comparing documents to find clues and make decisions.

blocks.title: Learning Unity by building a neighbourhood
blocks.text: Unity was the steepest part of the jam. The project went onto Unity Version Control on April 21; two days later our first house model sat alone on an empty plane, and by April 27 we had a night street, a suburban block from an asset pack and placeholder mannequins walking it. The final game reuses a first-person horror template (its inventory, lockpicking and readable papers) and tells the story on paper: a newspaper, an obituary, seven letters.

media.caption: April 23: our first house model, alone on an empty plane.
April 26: a lit night street and a placeholder mannequin.
April 27: the suburban block, from an asset pack.
The house at night in the Unity editor; the camera preview shows the marble maze on the couch.

blocks.title: Props from a sentence, characters from Mixamo
blocks.text: Our props started as words. For the pie we typed a description into Tripo and got a model back; text prompts were usually enough. The letters and the newspaper took two steps: we wrote the copy first, had GPT turn it into images, then had Tripo build the objects from those. make this line better While the grandmother and the cat were ready to go models downloaded from sketchfab, the player Candel, were also built from scratch from midjourney to gpt to 3D model, then move with Mixamo animations. The trouble was always the same two things, too many faces and textures that didn't come out right.

media.caption: The newspaper prop: the story is told on paper.

blocks.title: The rules underneath the scare
blocks.text:
About 6,000 lines of our own C# sit on top of the horror template without changing it; new systems plug in through small bridges, so the template's doors, inventory and state machine keep working. 

! System | What it does
Ghost cat | Waits at the porch and leads the way: click her and she meows, fades and reappears at the next waypoint; the last time, she leaves a charm.
Charms and pies | Every pickup is counted on screen. Enough pies unlock the pistol; the five charms are what the pool ritual needs.
The grandmother | Waits unseen in the hall closet until you open it, then hunts you. A trigger box around the house keeps her home: she chases past the door for four seconds, then is sent back to patrol. The axe only knocks her home; the pistol's one bullet ends her.
Two endings | The bullet ends her (Ending 1, told in crimson); five charms dropped into the pool release her (Ending 2, in amber).
Guidance | One controller reads the inventory every frame and moves the objective and hint on screen.
Puzzles | A two-phase marble maze, padlocked chests, a mailbox of bobby pins and letters.

blocks.title: Vibecoding is debugging, debugging, and debugging
blocks.text:
On May 7, two days before the showcase, Unity would only open our project in Safe Mode: 999+ compilation errors. The horror template had been imported twice, so every class in it existed twice (error CS0101).That night we fixed duplicate keys in the package lock and removed stray Windows thumbnail files from the project. After midnight the next sync brought hundreds of missing-prefab links. At 3:30 pm on May 8 the log finally read “All current bugs have been fixed”, and the last evening went to the opening and to putting the grandmother in.

Vibecoding made us faster and slower at once. The hardest part was communication: getting Claude to fix one thing without rewriting logic that already worked. And it only helped when the story was clear to us first. If we weren't sure what a scene was for, the AI wasn't either.

media.caption: May 7, 3:52 pm: the project would only open in Safe Mode.
999+ errors: the template's classes, defined twice (CS0101).
After midnight: hundreds of missing-prefab links.
The fix, commit by commit (e-mails blurred): my package-lock and thumbnail fixes on May 7, “All current bugs have been fixed” on May 8.

blocks.title: Player autonomy or linear storytelling?
blocks.text:
You pick the lock, the grandmother appears, and a ghost cat leads you through the house: a flashlight, the letters, a marble maze on the couch, a basement chest whose code is the date on her last letter. Then she starts hunting you.

Designing the story was harder than building it. A horror game has to guide players, or they freeze in a dark hallway and stop, and our scope was too big to tell a great branching story. So it runs in a line: A leads to B leads to C leads to D. We gave players two ways through: collect pies for a pistol with one bullet and erase her, or collect charms and set her spirit free. Despite the underlying story we designed, most of the gameplay revolves around avoiding the grandmother, who chases the player whenever they enter her line of sight. This works well as a horror mechanic, but the hidden story elements could be communicated more clearly.

media.caption: The grandmother suddenly jumps out of a box in the basement, startling the player with a jumpscare.

blocks.title: Demo Day!
blocks.text:
On May 9 the showcase ran all day in the SAI SoundTank at the Frances Searle Building: demos and judging in the morning, a panel, then free play until the awards. Each team had a table, and someone had to present to qualify. Four judges played: two game-design instructors, one from Northwestern and one from UChicago; the head of Night City, Chicago's indie game community space; and a sound designer for games. Our hint text wasn't enough on the floor. Being chased is distracting, so we stood next to players and talked them through what to do.

This is the first time I ever built a video game from scratch. Unity was our biggest lesson: a shared project breaks in ways a single file never does, through a doubled import, a lock file, two operating systems, and fixing it is part of making the game. I also took away how game logic holds a story together, how to tell a story well, and how much autonomy to leave to the player.
